summary.text: Define the candidate linear-recurrence sequence \(B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n\) and an auxiliary positive remainder sequence \(D\), and prove \(B_{k+1}^2=B_{k+2}B_k+D_k\) with \(0<D_k\le B_k\). This remainder bound makes \(\lceil B_{k+1}^2/B_k\rceil-1=B_{k+2}\), so induction identifies the originally defined sequence with \(B\), yielding the claimed recurrence and hence generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(k\ge 0\), \(a_{k+2}\) is the greatest integer for which
\[
\frac{a_{k+2}}{a_{k+1}}<\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}.
\]
All the terms that occur below are positive. Consequently, after multiplying by the positive denominator \(a_ka_{k+1}\), the displayed inequality is equivalent to
\[
a_{k+2}<\frac{a_{k+1}^2}{a_k}.
\]
For any real number \(x\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(x\) is \(\lceil x\rceil-1\), including when \(x\) itself is an integer. Hence the original rule is equivalently
\[
a_{k+2}=\left\lceil\frac{a_{k+1}^2}{a_k}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
We will prove that this nonlinear recurrence is exactly satisfied by the sequence arising from the proposed rational generating function.

Define an auxiliary sequence \((B_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
B_0=4,\qquad B_1=16,\qquad B_2=63,
\]
and
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
The first few values are
\[
B_3=4\cdot63-4=248,
\qquad
B_4=4\cdot248-16=976,
\]
as expected from the original-definition variant.

We first establish positivity and sufficient growth of \(B_n\). We claim that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
B_n>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad 3B_n\le B_{n+1}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=0,1,2\), these assertions follow directly from
\[
B_0=4,\quad B_1=16,\quad B_2=63,\quad B_3=248:
\]
indeed, \(12\le16\), \(48\le63\), and \(189\le248\).

For the induction step, suppose the assertions are known through the indices needed below. From (2),
\[
B_{k+3}=4B_{k+2}-B_k.
\]
The preceding growth inequalities imply in particular that \(B_k\le B_{k+2}\). Therefore
\[
B_{k+3}\ge 3B_{k+2}>0.
\]
Similarly,
\[
B_{k+4}=4B_{k+3}-B_{k+1}.
\]
Since the already established growth makes the sequence increasing, \(B_{k+1}\le B_{k+3}\), and hence
\[
B_{k+4}\ge3B_{k+3}.
\]
This proves (3) by strong induction. In particular, every subtraction in (2) has a nonnegative, in fact positive, result, so (2) may be read equally well as a recurrence in the positive integers. It also follows that \(B_n<B_{n+1}\) for every \(n\).

The key point is to control exactly how far the quotient \(B_{k+1}^2/B_k\) lies above the integer \(B_{k+2}\). For this purpose define a second sequence \((D_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
D_0=4,\qquad D_1=1,\qquad D_2=16,
\]
and
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{4}
\]
Every \(D_n\) is positive: this is immediate for the first three terms, and thereafter follows inductively from (4).

We next prove the determinant-type identity
\[
B_{k+1}^2=B_{k+2}B_k+D_k\qquad(k\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
To see why (4) is the relevant auxiliary recurrence, put
\[
E_k=B_{k+1}^2-B_{k+2}B_k.
\]
Direct calculation gives
\[
E_0=16^2-63\cdot4=4.
\]
Using \(B_3=248\),
\[
E_1=63^2-248\cdot16=3969-3968=1,
\]
and using \(B_4=976\),
\[
E_2=248^2-976\cdot63=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus \(E_0,E_1,E_2\) agree with \(D_0,D_1,D_2\).

Moreover, the \(E_k\) satisfy the same recurrence as the \(D_k\). Indeed, from (2),
\[
B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n,
\quad
B_{n+4}=4B_{n+3}-B_{n+1},
\quad
B_{n+5}=4B_{n+4}-B_{n+2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{n+3}
&=B_{n+4}^2-B_{n+5}B_{n+3}\\
&=(4B_{n+3}-B_{n+1})^2
 -\bigl(4(4B_{n+3}-B_{n+1})-B_{n+2}\bigr)B_{n+3}\\
&=B_{n+1}^2-4B_{n+1}B_{n+3}+B_{n+2}B_{n+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4E_{n+1}+E_n
&=4(B_{n+2}^2-B_{n+3}B_{n+1})
 +(B_{n+1}^2-B_{n+2}B_n)\\
&=B_{n+1}^2-4B_{n+1}B_{n+3}
 +B_{n+2}(4B_{n+2}-B_n)\\
&=B_{n+1}^2-4B_{n+1}B_{n+3}+B_{n+2}B_{n+3},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality again uses (2). Hence
\[
E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n.
\]
Because \(E\) and \(D\) have the same first three values and obey the same recurrence, induction gives \(E_k=D_k\) for every \(k\), which is exactly (5).

For the ceiling in (1), positivity of \(D_k\) is not quite enough: we also need an upper bound on the remainder. We claim that
\[
D_k\le B_k\qquad(k\ge0). \tag{6}
\]
This holds initially because
\[
D_0=4=B_0,
\qquad D_1=1\le16=B_1,
\qquad D_2=16\le63=B_2.
\]
Suppose inductively that \(D_n\le B_n\) and \(D_{n+1}\le B_{n+1}\). By (4),
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n
\le4B_{n+1}+B_n. \tag{7}
\]
We compare this with \(B_{n+3}=4B_{n+2}-B_n\). The growth result (3) gives both \(B_n\le B_{n+1}\) and \(B_{n+2}\ge3B_{n+1}\). Consequently,
\[
4B_{n+1}+2B_n
\le6B_{n+1}
\le12B_{n+1}
\le4B_{n+2}.
\]
Rearranging this inequality yields
\[
4B_{n+1}+B_n\le4B_{n+2}-B_n=B_{n+3}.
\]
Together with (7), this proves \(D_{n+3}\le B_{n+3}\). Strong induction proves (6) for all \(k\).

We can now evaluate the nonlinear recurrence exactly. Identity (5) says
\[
B_{k+1}^2=B_{k+2}B_k+D_k,
\]
while positivity and (6) say
\[
0<D_k\le B_k. \tag{8}
\]
Dividing by the positive integer \(B_k\), we obtain
\[
\frac{B_{k+1}^2}{B_k}
=B_{k+2}+\frac{D_k}{B_k},
\qquad 0<\frac{D_k}{B_k}\le1.
\]
Thus the ceiling of this number is always \(B_{k+2}+1\). This remains true in the endpoint case \(D_k=B_k\), when the quotient is already the integer \(B_{k+2}+1\). Therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{B_{k+1}^2}{B_k}\right\rceil-1=B_{k+2} \qquad(k\ge0). \tag{9}
\]
Equivalently, because \(B_k,B_{k+1}>0\), \(B_{k+2}\) is precisely the greatest integer \(m\) such that
\[
\frac m{B_{k+1}}<\frac{B_{k+1}}{B_k}.
\]
So \(B\) obeys the original extremal consecutive-ratio rule.

It remains to identify \(B\) with the recursively defined original sequence \(a\). We use strong induction on \(n\). The equality is immediate for \(n=0,1\), since both sequences begin with \(4,16\). If \(n=k+2\) and the equality is known at all smaller indices, then (1), the induction hypothesis, and (9) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+2}
&=\left\lceil\frac{a_{k+1}^2}{a_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=\left\lceil\frac{B_{k+1}^2}{B_k}\right\rceil-1\\
&=B_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a_n=B_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{10}
\]
In particular, the original sequence has initial values
\[
a_0=4,
\qquad a_1=16,
\qquad a_2=\left\lceil\frac{16^2}{4}\right\rceil-1=63,
\]
and, by (2) and (10), satisfies
\[
a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}\qquad(n\ge3). \tag{11}
\]

Finally, let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. Multiplying by \(1-4x+x^3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) for every \(n\ge3\) is
\[
a_n-4a_{n-1}+a_{n-3}=0
\]
by (11). The three remaining coefficients are
\[
[x^0]:a_0=4,
\]
\[
[x^1]:a_1-4a_0=16-16=0,
\]
and
\[
[x^2]:a_2-4a_1=63-64=-1.
\]
Hence
\[
(1-4x+x^3)A(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{A(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves that the sequence produced by the original, always-“greatest integer below the preceding ratio” definition is exactly the sequence with the conjectured generating function.
